findings.evidence: "However, reimbursement is not available without a completed receipt" (Eligibility); "The finance office deposits the amount within one pay cycle" (Reimbursement Amounts); "You record the stipend item on the request form. Finance reconciles the stipend item against the request log each month. Payroll releases the stipend item amount after that monthly review" (Terminology Notes)
findings.fix: Pick one term for the benefit payment (for example, the stipend) and use it consistently everywhere the document currently substitutes reimbursement, deposit, or stipend item for the same concept, reserving the other words for genuinely distinct ideas if any remain.
findings.location: Eligibility paragraph 2; Reimbursement Amounts; Terminology Notes
findings.violation: The document uses stipend, reimbursement, and stipend item interchangeably for what reads as the same underlying benefit payment, with no defined-terms section or stated equivalence reconciling them, so a reader cannot tell whether 'reimbursement' and 'the stipend item' name the thing already introduced as 'the stipend' or something new.

findings.evidence: "If the position counts as full-time, the stipend can apply. If the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, the stipend can apply. If the request arrives before the benefit year ends, the stipend can apply. Only once every condition above is met does the home-office equipment stipend become available to the employee."
findings.fix: State the governing rule first (for example, 'The stipend is available only when the employee meets all of the following conditions:'), then list the three conditions underneath it.
findings.violation: The paragraph opens with three separate conditional sentences before the fourth sentence finally states the governing rule (that all three conditions must hold together), so the reader has to hold three unresolved conditionals in mind and cannot tell until the last sentence that they were cumulative rather than independent triggers.

findings.evidence: 36-word sentence, 4 subordinate-clause markers: Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email.
findings.fix: Split the sentence at a subordinate-clause boundary.
findings.violation: The sentence runs to 36 words with 4 subordinate-clause markers, longer than the reader can hold in mind on a single pass.

findings.evidence: "The people operations office publishes the reimbursement log each quarter" (Program Overview) versus "The benefits team publishes the reimbursement log after every open enrollment period" (Overview)
findings.fix: Merge the two overview sections into one and state once, consistently, which team publishes the reimbursement log and on what cadence.
findings.location: Program Overview (top) and the second Overview section (near the end)
findings.violation: Two sections about the identical artifact, the reimbursement log, attribute its publication to different teams on different schedules with no signal reconciling the two accounts, so a reader who reads both cannot state a single consistent answer to who publishes the log or how often, which is the exact question an overview section exists to settle.

findings.evidence: "You record the stipend item on the request form. Finance reconciles the stipend item against the request log each month. Payroll releases the stipend item amount after that monthly review. Also, you submit the request in the portal. You track its status there until the payment clears."
findings.fix: Reorder the sentences to follow the actual sequence (submit the request, then Finance/Payroll process it) and keep a single tracked subject across consecutive sentences instead of alternating between the employee and each internal team every sentence.
findings.violation: The paragraph's subject changes on nearly every sentence (you, Finance, Payroll, you, You) with no sentence picking up the topic the previous one just established, and the fourth sentence ('you submit the request') introduces a step that chronologically precedes the three processing sentences before it, so the reader has to re-orient at each boundary and then reconstruct the actual order of events.

findings.evidence: "Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email."
findings.fix: End the sentence on the fact the reader most needs: that the backup reviewer was not told sign-off was required, and move the confirmation-email detail to its own sentence or drop it.
findings.violation: The sentence's most important new fact, that the backup reviewer was never told the request needs their sign-off, which is what is actually holding up the process, is buried in the middle, and the sentence instead ends on an unrelated detail, the portal releasing a confirmation email, that the document never returns to.

findings.evidence: The request is reviewed within two business days.
findings.fix: Rewrite the sentence in active voice, naming the actor that performs the action.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a be-verb plus past-participle passive construction in a context where the actor is recoverable and worth naming directly.

findings.evidence: Also, the deposit happens in order to offset costs the employee already paid at this point in time.
findings.fix: Replace the wordy phrase with its plain equivalent (for example, because for due to the fact that).
findings.violation: The sentence uses a wordy construction from the fixed wordy-phrase list that a shorter equivalent would carry with no loss of meaning.

findings.evidence: However, reimbursement is not available without a completed receipt.
findings.fix: Restate the sentence with at most one negation, or recast it as a positive statement.
findings.violation: 2 negation markers from the fixed negation list co-occur in one clause, so the reader has to work out the statement's logical sign before understanding it.

findings.fix: Replace the heading with text specific enough to be found by scanning.
findings.violation: The heading text matches the fixed list of non-specific heading labels, so a reader scanning headings cannot tell whether the section applies to them.

findings.evidence: The manager approves items pursuant to internal discretion, notwithstanding the standard review checklist.
findings.fix: Replace the jargon term with a plain equivalent, or define it at first use.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a legal or foreign-language jargon term from the fixed list with no plain-language definition in the same or the following sentence.
